title: Rube Goldberg Machines — Simple Machines & Energy

script.x: Greet students warmly as they join. Ask how their week has been.
script.a: Keep it light — names, a smile, one quick share each. Sets the participation norm before any content.

chunks.name: Can you trace this crazy machine?

items.title: What does it finally DO? 🤔
items.content:
Each lettered step makes the next one happen.
Where does the chain end up?

script.x: Point to each step A→E and let students call out what happens next. Build suspense toward the bowl at the end.
So what is the ONE simple job this whole contraption does?
script.a: It feeds a pet / fills a bowl — a tiny job done in a wonderfully complicated way.

script.x: Name it: this is a **Rube Goldberg Machine** — a silly invention that does a simple job through a chain reaction.

items.title: Before we build, two secrets 🔑
items.content:
Every Rube Goldberg machine is built from just **two** ideas:

**1.** Energy transfer — each step passes energy to the next.
**2.** Simple machines — the 6 tools that make wacky steps.

items.text: Hold the two secrets here as the spine of the whole lesson. Everything after this fills them in.

script.x: How does step A make step B happen — what is actually being passed along?
script.a: Energy! The motion/force of one object moves the next. That's secret #1.

script.x: Preview secret #2: the wacky steps are built from 6 simple machines. We'll master them one by one.

items.text: Don't define them yet — just name them and build anticipation. Each gets its own hands-on round.

script.x: Read out the 6 simple machines. Tell students each one unlocks a new kind of wacky step.
Which of these have you already seen today — in a playground, a kitchen, a bike?
script.a: Take a few — ramps, see-saws, wheels, bottle-cap openers. Primes recognition before the science.

items.name: Inclined Plane — Energy Explorer
items.html:
Energy of the ball

Potential100%
Kinetic0%
Drag up / down to tilt the ramp
26°

items.title: Roll it down 🎢
items.content:
Drag the angle, then release the ball.
Watch the energy bars flip as it rolls.

items.text: Let a student drive: change the ramp angle and release. Ask them to narrate the energy bars.

script.x: Open the model. Show how a student takes control to change the angle and release the ball.
Make the ramp gentler, then steeper. When is the climb up easier — and what happens to the roll down?
script.a: Gentler = easier to move up, slower roll down. Same height, same energy, different effort.

items.title: The inclined plane
items.content:
A ramp moves objects between two levels without lifting them straight up.
A gentler slope = an easier climb.

script.x: Recap the trick: inclined planes move things up or down. In a chain, a ramp is a great way to start a ball moving.

items.prompt: A ball sits at the top of a ramp, not moving. What energy does it mostly have?

script.x: Ball at the top, still — what energy?
script.a: **Gravitational PE.** It's high up and not moving yet.

items.prompt: As the ball rolls down the ramp, its energy mainly transforms into…

script.x: Rolling down — PE turns into what?
script.a: **Kinetic energy.** Height converts to motion; energy changes form, never vanishes.

items.name: Energy Transfer Visualizer
items.html:
Drag the ball up, then press Play
Drag up / down to set the drop height
Gravitational PE
Kinetic energy
Transferred to cart

items.title: Drop & transfer ⚙️
items.content:
Press Play: a falling ball hits a cart on wheels.
Follow the energy from object to object.

items.text: Press Play. Pause on impact — this is the moment energy moves from the ball to the wheeled cart.

script.x: Open the Energy Transfer model. Play it once all the way through.
Name the energy at three moments: ball up high, ball falling, ball hitting the cart.
script.a: High = PE; falling = KE; impact = KE transferred into the cart. One clean chain of transformations.

items.title: The wheel & axle
items.content: A wheel turns around a rod (the axle), letting heavy things roll instead of drag.

script.x: Recap: the wheel & axle turns a hard drag into an easy roll — perfect for moving a load across your machine.

items.prompt: A heavy ball falls and strikes a cart, which rolls away. What happened to the ball's energy?
options: It transferred to the cart as kinetic energy

script.x: Ball hits cart, cart rolls — where did the energy go?
script.a: **Transferred** to the cart as kinetic energy. Energy moved from one object to the next — secret #1 in action.

items.prompt: Why does a wheel & axle make a heavy load easier to move?
options: It lets the load roll instead of drag

script.x: Why is rolling easier than dragging?
script.a: The wheel turns on the axle, so the load **rolls** with far less resistance.

items.name: Lever — Fulcrum Lab
items.html:
Drag left ↔ right (or use the slider) to move the fulcrum, then drop the weight to launch the ball. Fulcrum closer to the rock = easier lift.
centred

items.title: Find the sweet spot ⚖️
items.content:
Slide the fulcrum, then drop the weight to launch the ball.
Where is lifting easiest?

items.text: Let students try several fulcrum positions before dropping the weight. They should FEEL the trade-off.

script.x: Open the Lever model. Demonstrate one fulcrum position, then hand control to a student.
Predict before you drop: which fulcrum position will fling the ball the FARTHEST?
script.a: Fulcrum near the load/heavy side gives the long arm a big swing — biggest launch. Take predictions, then test.

items.title: The lever
items.content:
A beam that turns on a fulcrum. A load on one side, effort on the other.
Fulcrum closer to the load = easier lift (and a bigger launch).

script.x: Recap: levers lift heavy loads and launch light ones. A catapult step is just a lever used for launching.

items.prompt: On a lever, moving the fulcrum closer to the heavy load makes lifting it…

script.x: Fulcrum closer to the load — easier or harder to lift?
script.a: **Easier.** Less effort is needed when the fulcrum sits near the load.

items.prompt: In the launch model, the falling weight gives the ball its push. That push is a transfer of…

script.x: The dropping weight launches the ball — what's transferred?
script.a: **Kinetic energy** — the weight's motion becomes the ball's motion and it flies.

items.title: Pull down, lift up 🪝
items.content: A grooved wheel and a rope. Pulling **down** on one side lifts the load **up** on the other.

items.text: Show how the direction of the force flips: you pull down, the load rises. That's the whole trick.

script.x: Walk through the pulley diagram: rope over a wheel, load on one end.
If you pull the rope DOWN, which way does the load go — and why is that handy?
script.a: It goes UP. Pulling down is easier (you can use your weight), so a pulley redirects force to your advantage.

items.prompt: What does a pulley mainly do to the force you apply?

script.x: What does a pulley do to your force?
script.a: **Changes its direction** — pull down, load goes up.

items.title: A ramp in disguise 🌀
items.content: A screw is an **inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder** — a long gentle ramp packed into a small space.

items.text: Connect back to the inclined plane: the screw is the SAME idea, just coiled. Lowers things gently.

script.x: Trace the spiral on the screw diagram with your finger — show it's one long ramp wound up.
Which earlier machine is hiding inside a screw?
script.a: The **inclined plane**. A screw is a ramp wrapped around a cylinder — great for lowering something gently.

items.prompt: A screw is best described as…
options: An inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder

script.x: What simple machine is a screw built from?
script.a: An **inclined plane** wrapped around a cylinder.

items.title: Push in, force splits 🔪
items.content: A wedge takes one push and **redirects** it sideways to split or push things apart.

items.text: Show the single downward push becoming two sideways forces. Door stops and axe-heads are wedges.

script.x: Use the wedge diagram: one arrow in at the top, two arrows out at the sides.
Where have you seen a wedge doing real work?
script.a: Knife, axe, door stop, the front of a boat. One push in → force pushes outward to split or hold.

items.prompt: What does a wedge do to the force you push with?
options: Redirects it sideways to split things

script.x: What does a wedge do with your push?
script.a: **Redirects it sideways** to split or push things apart.

items.title: Two secrets, six tools ✅
items.content:
You now know all **6 simple machines** and how each one transfers energy into a wacky step.
This is your trick sheet for building.

script.x: Celebrate: bootcamp complete. Run through the trick sheet — what each machine lets you do in a chain.
Keep this slide handy during the build; students will pick steps straight off this toolbox.

items.title: The Engineering Design Process
items.content:
Engineers don't guess — they loop:
**Ask → Imagine → Plan → Create → Improve.**
You'll use the same five steps.

script.x: When engineers face a brand-new machine, do they just try random ideas?
script.a: No — they follow a process: Ask, Imagine, Plan, Create, Improve. Test, learn, improve.

script.x: Introduce the EDP cycle. Stress that engineers rarely get it right the first time — improving is the point.

items.title: The challenge 🐶
items.content:
Build a chain reaction that presses the feeder button.

**• Use at least 4 simple machines
• Create 3+ energy transformations
• Run with no human help once started**

script.x: Read the mission and the design criteria. This is the **Ask** step — define the problem clearly.
In your own words: what exactly does your machine have to make happen at the very end?
script.a: Press the feeder button so the pet is fed — using a chain of at least 4 machines.

items.name: Chain-Reaction Sandbox — Feed the Pet
items.html:
Tap a machine, then tap a glowing slot to place it
GOAL: build the chain that
presses the feeder button 🐶
0 / 3 placed Inclined plane Lever Wheel & axle

items.title: Imagine → Plan → Create 🛠️
items.content:
Tap a machine, drop it into a glowing slot, then press **Run** to test your chain.
Didn't reach the bowl? **Improve** and run again.

items.text: Hand a student control via Interact. Let the class plan the order before placing. Encourage a retry after the first run — that's the Improve step.

script.x: Open the sandbox. Model placing one machine, then give students control to build and run their own chain.
Your chain didn't reach the bowl — what's your ONE change before the next run?
script.a: Any reasoned tweak: reorder steps, swap a machine, adjust placement. Reward iterating over guessing — that's Improve.

script.x: The model tracks placement and a successful run; for the full criteria (4+ machines, 3+ transformations) have students tally on paper.

chunks.name: Show & Tell — you're a Mechanical Engineer!

items.title: Share your machine 🎬
items.content: Record a short show-and-tell: what your machine does, which simple machines you used, and the trickiest step you solved.

items.title: What's next
items.content: You designed, built, tested, and improved a real chain reaction — exactly how mechanical engineers work.

script.x: Have students present their machine in one minute: the job, the machines used, the hardest fix.
STEM spotlight: mechanical engineers design machines we use every day — bikes, cars, even toys.
Tell me one thing you can do now that you couldn't before this project.
script.a: Anything from 'name the 6 machines' to 'plan a chain reaction' to 'spot energy transfers'. End on their growth.
